j.q: Why do leaves change colour in the fall?
j.a: Green comes from chlorophyll, which helps leaves make food. In fall trees stop making it, so the yellow and orange hiding underneath finally show.

c.q: Fold paper in half 42 times. How thick is it?
c.a: Thick enough to reach the Moon. Each fold doubles it: 0.1 mm × 2⁴² ≈ 440,000 km. The real-world record is only 12 folds.

j.a: Sunlight has every colour in it. Air scatters blue light much more than red, so blue bounces all over the sky and into our eyes.

c.q: If the sky is blue, why are sunsets orange and red?
c.a: At sunset, light passes through far more air to reach you. Most of the blue gets scattered away, leaving the reds and oranges.

j.a: Bees sip nectar from flowers and pass it between them, store it in wax cells, then fan it with their wings until most of the water dries off.

c.q: About how many flowers do bees visit to make one jar of honey?
c.a: Roughly 2 million flowers — and the hive flies more than twice around the Earth to do it.

j.q: How many legs does a spider have? Is it an insect?
j.a: Eight legs, so no! Insects have six. Spiders are arachnids, like scorpions and ticks.

c.q: Why can't you tickle yourself?
c.a: Your brain predicts exactly what your own hand will do and turns the feeling down. Tickling works best as a surprise.

j.q: Why does the Moon change shape?
j.a: It doesn't really! The Moon is always a ball, half lit by the Sun. As it circles Earth we see different amounts of the lit half.

c.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
c.a: The Moon spins exactly once for every trip around Earth, so the same face always points at us. It's called tidal locking.

j.q: Where does a puddle go when it dries up?
j.a: It evaporates — the water turns into an invisible gas and floats into the air. Later it can become clouds and rain.

c.q: Could you be drinking the same water a dinosaur drank?
c.a: Very likely! Earth keeps recycling its water through clouds, rain, rivers and oceans. Hardly any is new or lost.

j.q: What's the biggest animal that has ever lived?
j.a: The blue whale — bigger than any dinosaur. It can be about 30 metres long, as long as two and a half school buses.

c.q: A blue whale's heart is about the size of what?
c.a: A bumper car, weighing around 180 kg. Toronto's Royal Ontario Museum preserved a real one.

j.a: Rain slowly washes tiny bits of salt out of rocks. Rivers carry it to the sea, and when seawater evaporates, the salt stays behind.

c.q: Rivers carry salt into the Great Lakes too. Why are they fresh?
c.a: Water also flows OUT of the Great Lakes, down the St. Lawrence to the ocean, so salt never builds up. The ocean has no exit.

j.q: Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
j.a: Light travels much faster than sound. Count the seconds between flash and boom, divide by 3, and that's about how many km away the storm is.

c.q: How hot is a lightning bolt?
c.a: About 30,000 °C — roughly five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

j.a: Billions of tiny water droplets or ice crystals, so small and light that they float.

c.q: How much does a puffy cumulus cloud weigh?
c.a: About 500,000 kg — as heavy as around 100 elephants. It floats because that water is spread over a huge space.

j.q: Why do onions make you cry?
j.a: Cutting an onion releases a gas that stings your eyes. Your eyes make tears to wash it away.

c.q: Why does chilling an onion first help?
c.a: Cold slows the chemical reaction that makes the stinging gas, so less of it reaches your eyes.

j.a: Fish have gills that pull oxygen out of the water as it flows over them.

c.q: How do fish survive all winter under the ice?
c.a: Water is heaviest at about 4 °C, so that warmer water sinks to the bottom. The ice on top acts like a blanket and the lake doesn't freeze solid.

j.q: Why does a rubbed balloon stick to the wall?
j.a: Rubbing moves tiny charges called electrons onto the balloon. That static electricity pulls it toward the wall.

c.q: Why do you get more static shocks in winter?
c.a: Cold winter air is very dry. Without moisture to let charge leak away, it builds up on you until — zap — it jumps to a doorknob.

j.q: How long does sunlight take to reach us?
j.a: About 8 minutes. When you see the Sun, you're seeing it as it was 8 minutes ago!

c.q: When you see a star, are you seeing it as it is now?
c.a: No — you're seeing old light. Light from some stars you can see left them hundreds of years ago.

j.a: Scientists think stripes help keep biting flies away — flies get confused and have trouble landing on them.

c.q: What colour is a polar bear's skin?
c.a: Black! Its fur looks white, but each hair is actually see-through.

j.a: Tiny muscles pull your hairs upright when you're cold or scared. For furry animals it traps warm air; for us it's mostly a leftover.

c.q: Why do your fingers wrinkle in the bath?
c.a: Your nerves shrink blood vessels in your fingertips, wrinkling the skin. Scientists think it may help you grip wet things.

j.q: How does a caterpillar become a butterfly?
j.a: It makes a chrysalis, and inside its body breaks down and rebuilds into a butterfly. It's called metamorphosis.

c.q: Where do Ontario's monarch butterflies go every winter?
c.a: To mountain forests in central Mexico — more than 3,000 km away. None of them has ever made the trip before.

j.q: Why do we have leap years?
j.a: Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to go around the Sun. Every four years those quarters add up to an extra day: February 29.

c.q: Is 2100 a leap year?
c.a: No! Years ending in 00 skip the leap day unless they divide by 400. So 2000 was a leap year, but 2100 won't be.

j.a: Venus, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Venus's thick clouds trap heat like a blanket — it's about 465 °C.

c.q: On Venus, which is longer: a day or a year?
c.a: A day! Venus spins so slowly that one turn takes 243 Earth days, but its year is only 225 Earth days.

j.a: Their wings became flippers for swimming. Penguins "fly" underwater instead!

c.q: What's the fastest animal on Earth?
c.a: The peregrine falcon. Diving for prey it can top 300 km/h. Peregrines even nest on tall Toronto buildings.

j.q: Why does your voice sound different in a recording?
j.a: When you talk you hear yourself through the air AND through the bones in your head, which sounds deeper. A recording only has the air part.

c.q: Why does helium make your voice squeaky?
c.a: Sound travels nearly three times faster in helium than in air, which changes the tone. Your vocal cords don't change at all.

j.a: Bending one breaks a little tube inside. Two chemicals mix and make light without getting hot.

c.q: Why does a glow stick last longer in the freezer?
c.a: Cold slows down the chemical reaction, so it glows dimmer but for much longer.

j.q: How many bones are in your body?
j.a: Adults have 206. Babies are born with around 300 — some join together as they grow.

c.q: What's the smallest bone in your body?
c.a: The stirrup (stapes) in your ear — about the size of a grain of rice. It helps you hear.

j.a: Each kernel has a tiny drop of water inside. Heat turns it to steam, pressure builds, and — POP — the kernel bursts inside out.

c.q: Why do some kernels never pop?
c.a: Their shells are cracked or they're too dry, so steam escapes instead of building up pressure.

j.q: Where does the name Toronto come from?
j.a: Probably from the Mohawk word "tkaronto", meaning "where there are trees standing in the water."

c.q: What was Toronto called before 1834?
c.a: York — nicknamed "Muddy York." It became the City of Toronto in 1834.

j.q: How tall is the CN Tower?
j.a: 553 metres. For 32 years it was the tallest free-standing structure in the world.

c.q: How long does the CN Tower elevator take to the LookOut?
c.a: About 58 seconds, climbing at roughly 22 km/h.

j.a: To find insects hiding in wood, to dig nest holes, and to drum loud messages to other woodpeckers.

c.q: How fast can a woodpecker peck?
c.a: Up to about 20 times per second.

j.a: Sunlight shines through raindrops. Each drop bends the light and splits it into colours.

c.q: Where must the Sun be for you to see a rainbow?
c.a: Behind you and low in the sky. A rainbow is always on the opposite side of the sky from the Sun.

j.a: A dog's nose is thousands of times better than ours. Sniffing is how they "read" who's been around.

c.q: Why are dogs' noses wet?
c.a: A damp nose catches smell particles better. Dogs make mucus and lick their noses to keep them wet.

j.a: When water freezes, its molecules lock into a pattern with more space between them, so ice is lighter than the same amount of water.

c.q: Why do water pipes sometimes burst in winter?
c.a: Water expands by about 9% when it freezes. Trapped in a pipe, it pushes hard enough to crack metal.

j.a: Jupiter. More than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.

c.q: How long would it take to drive to the Moon at 100 km/h?
c.a: About 160 days of non-stop driving — over five months.

j.a: Scientists aren't totally sure! One idea is that yawning helps cool your brain. And yawns are catching — did you just yawn?

c.q: Why are yawns contagious?
c.a: It may be linked to empathy: people catch yawns more often from family and friends than from strangers.

j.a: Roots soak up water from the soil, and it travels up tiny tubes in the stem all the way to the leaves.

c.q: How does water reach the top of a 100-metre tree without a pump?
c.a: Water evaporating from the leaves pulls the water column up behind it, like sipping through a very long straw.

j.a: Snowflakes are clear ice, but their many tiny edges bounce light in every direction, mixing all the colours into white.

c.q: Is it true no two snowflakes are alike?
c.a: For big, complex flakes, practically yes — each takes its own path through the cloud, so an exact match is extremely unlikely.

j.q: How fast is the Earth spinning?
j.a: In Toronto we're whizzing around at about 1,200 km/h! We don't feel it because everything spins with us.

c.q: If Earth spins so fast, why do you land in the same spot when you jump?
c.a: You're already moving with the Earth and you keep that speed in the air — like jumping inside a moving train.

j.a: There's little food in winter, so bears sleep through it. Their heartbeat slows and they live off fat stored in the fall.

c.q: How long can a black bear go without eating or drinking?
c.a: Up to about seven months in its winter den. Its body even recycles waste into protein.

j.a: Mostly when they're happy and relaxed — but sometimes when hurt or scared, to calm themselves. Muscles in the voice box twitch very fast.

c.q: Which is stronger for its weight: spider silk or steel?
c.a: Some spider silk! Weight for weight it can beat steel — and it stretches too.

j.q: Why do we need to sleep?
j.a: Sleep helps your body grow and repair, and helps your brain sort and save what you learned today.

c.q: How much sleep do experts recommend for teenagers?
c.a: 8 to 10 hours a night. Teen body clocks naturally shift later, which is why early mornings feel so hard.

j.a: Their wings are shaped and tilted so moving air pushes them up. Engines keep the plane moving fast enough for the air to keep lifting.

c.q: Why are flights from Toronto to Europe often faster than flights back?
c.a: The jet stream — a fast river of wind high up — usually blows west to east, giving eastbound planes a tailwind.

j.q: Which grow faster: fingernails or toenails?
j.a: Fingernails — about three to four times faster than toenails.

c.q: Where does the oxygen we breathe come from?
c.a: Plants and tiny ocean plankton make it. Scientists estimate ocean plankton produce about half of Earth's oxygen.
